options.P1: One object with a role flag — the axis is an ordinary attribute, marked
options.P2: Two objects — a dedicated option/axis object beside the attribute system
options.BOTH: Both mechanisms, required together (value written twice)
options.NONE: Neither — no axis object exists to classify

subtallies.name: (b) Value storage — where a member's axis value lives
(d) D5 — who picks the axes (10 of 13 covered)
cells: the family chooses from the gated set

rows.shape: The discriminator is an ordinary attribute: color, shirt_size, number_of_items are plain schema properties, no different from item_weight. The whole variant mechanism is three ordinary attributes in the variations property group: parentage_level, child_parent_sku_relationship, variation_theme. The product type carries a list of eligible themes, not attributes; ItemVariationTheme.attributes is “names of the Amazon catalog item attributes” — array of string, names not $refs. The child's axis value sits in the same attributes map as everything else: "parentage_level":[{"value":"child"}] … "color":[{"value":"Red"}]. Hedge: the theme token ≠ the attribute name (SIZE resolves to shirt_size), so three strings exist per axis; the per-type theme enum is the legacy-XSD shape, ItemVariationTheme.theme is a bare string with no enum. First-party 2026-09-21: ItemVariationTheme.theme is a string with example "COLOR_NAME/STYLE_NAME" and no enum; attributes is < string > array; the stated purpose of a family is “a single detail page experience.”

rows.h: separate store, with an opt-in bridge back
rows.shape: ProductOption (7 fields: own id, name free text, position, values, optionValues, linkedMetafield), ProductOptionValue (6 fields: own id, hasVariants, linkedMetafieldValue, swatch), SelectedOption {name, value, optionValue: ProductOptionValue!}. ProductVariantSetInput.optionValues is the only non-null field across the whole product-create input. The one axis that generates variants is free text, bound to neither the taxonomy nor metafields unless you opt in via linkedMetafield (“currently in early access”; needs a list.metaobject_reference definition; linking shopify.color-pattern was refused while Product.category was null, accepted once set). Options are reached only through their product (productOptionsCreate(productId!)) — values per product, no shop-level option registry (counter-search: “Not found”).

“Use all standard variants: specify the standard [color], [pattern], [material], [age_group], [gender] and [size] attributes in addition to variant option [variant_option] even when these are part of the set of variant-identifying properties.” — under Minimum requirements, disapproval-backed. VariantOption is nested inside message ProductAttributes (ProductAttributes.VariantOption) — a repeated field, not a resource; name and value free text ≤250 chars, name unvalidated (the nonsense token qzxjvwkmp persisted). Nothing retrieved requires the two written values to be equal. Google publishes five different lists of which attributes are axes; no closed set.

rows.h: ambiguous on declaration · same store on value
rows.shape: Declaration is a child container with no identity: Specification — “used to specify product aspects for which variations within an inventory item group vary, and the order in which they appear” — no id, no URI, reachable only through its group (P2-shaped). But eligibility is a boolean on an ordinary category aspect: aspectEnabledForVariations on 197,046 of 197,046 aspects, true 73,833 / false 123,213 (P1-shaped) — “Not all aspects are allowed as a pivoting aspect.” Value storage unambiguous: “Each member of the inventory item group should have these same aspect names specified through the product.aspects container”; case-sensitive; on Trading the axis set is the same ns:NameValueListArrayType as ordinary Item Specifics.

rows.h: by name; a stated departure from #11031's “cannot be assigned”
rows.shape: The axis is an attribute name carried as a string in an array on each member — no object, no identifier: valueId 0 · attributeId 0 · $ref 0 over 451 MB. Four fields travel together on 6,957 of 6,967 types: variantGroupId (string 1..300), variantAttributeNames (array of a per-type enum, minItems 1, no max), isPrimaryVariant (["No","Yes"]), swatchImages[].swatchVariantAttribute. The axis value is an ordinary attribute value inside the same Visible.<ProductType> node, copied per item ("flavor":"Peppermint" / "Spearmint", both with "variantGroupId":"001960968586AX6"). Counter-fact carried: 280 types list 18,737 axis names that are not their own type's attributes, against the vendor's own rule; the swatch enum differs from the axis enum on 1,711 types (24.6 %).

rows.h: two disjoint namespaces; weaker typing on the axis side
rows.shape: Over all 92 records (1.7 MB) the number containing both attribute_id and variation_id is 0. No attribute carries an axis flag (is_axis 0, is_variation 0 — with the control that mandatory, is_oem, support_search_value do appear). The axis catalogue is a separate three-level tree: get_variations(category_id) → standardise_variation_list[] {variation_id, variation_name, variation_group_list[] {variation_group_id, variation_option_list[] {variation_option_id, variation_option_name}}}. Governance is a sentinel on both sides: custom variation → variation_id=0 + variation_name; custom attribute value → value_id=0 + original_value_name. Typing asymmetric: an attribute value is typed and carries a unit; a variation option is a bare label (value_unit 0, format_type 0 in the variation corpus).

rows.h: era-split, opposite directions — Era B (live) is P1
rows.shape: Era A — P2: a global axis catalogue by id: get_variant?cat_id= → variant_details[] {variant_id, has_unit, identifier, name, status, is_primary, units[] {variant_unit_id, unit_values[] {variant_unit_value_id, value, hex, icon}}} + variant_id_combinations; the attribute system is a different endpoint (Annotation). Era B — P1, the clearest role-flag instance in the thirteen: one call serves both roles, attributes[].type: SALES_PROPERTY | PRODUCT_PROPERTY — “SALES_PROPERTY: sales attributes that define product variants; PRODUCT_PROPERTY: product attributes that describe the product as a whole.” The flag scopes four sibling fields (is_requried, is_customizable, requirement_conditions, is_multiple_selection apply only to PRODUCT_PROPERTY). Consumed on different objects: product_attributes at Product depth 0, skus[].sales_attributes on the SKU. Asymmetric: a custom axis name is allowed (≤20 chars, id auto-generated), a custom product attribute is refused (12052247). A global↔local translation table sales_attribute_mappings exists (open).

CatalogItemOption (5: name, display_name, description, show_colors, values) and CatalogItemOptionValue (5: item_option_id, name, description, color, ordinal) are first-class CatalogObject types with their own ids — “a list of options (such as a color or size of a T-shirt) that can be assigned to item variations.” The value is a shared row referenced by id: the variation carries only {item_option_id, item_option_value_id}, and the option is reusable across items. Whether a custom attribute could ever be an axis is not stated; the governance vocabulary (enforce, allowed, enum, selection, maxLength) fires only on custom-attribute schemas, never on option schemas. Separate query classes for options (CatalogQueryItemsForItemOptions) vs custom-attribute search.

rows.h: the vendor says it migrated here from P1
rows.shape: “Several methods … have a version taking a ProductVariationAttribute parameter, and another deprecated version accepting a ObjectAttributeDefinition … The latter are historical leftovers from when object attributes were used directly as the basis for variation, and the value lists were stored directly on the ObjectAttributeDefinition. … values are now stored on the ProductVariationAttribute.” ProductVariationAttribute = 3 properties (attributeID, displayName, ID); every one corresponds to exactly one ObjectAttributeDefinition. Value side has a shared/local switch: VariationAttribute.shared: boolean, shared-variation-attribute reference vs a local inline copy. The only record stating a migration between the options — P1 → P2, because of value lists on a shared definition.

rows.h: same store; axes immutable once set
rows.shape: No Axis entity, table or column (0 hits in Attribute.orm.yml / Attribute.php; control 117 hits in Pim/Structure). axes and attributes both target AttributeInterface; “is an axis” = a row in pim_catalog_variant_attribute_set_has_axes. Eligibility is a static 5-element type list — pim_catalog_metric, pim_catalog_simpleselect, pim_catalog_boolean, pim_reference_data_simpleselect, akeneo_reference_entity — intersected with the family's own attributes, minus localizable/scopable/locale-specific/unique ones. Value in raw_values like every other value. Cost: axis-value comparison stringifies ((string)$value, joined with ',', mb_strtolower; metric as '%.4F %s'). Every axis is force-added to the same set's attributes — the two roles are structurally inseparable.

No axis object: an axis is an ordinary attribute carrying one boolean — WC_Product_Attribute.$data = ['id'=>0,'name'=>'','options'=>[],'position'=>0,'visible'=>false,'variation'=>false]. The flag is per (product, attribute), not per definition: the same global pa_flavour is variation:false on product 22 and true on product 10 — shape 1's per-family dimension row, as a boolean inside a serialised blob. Cost: one global value has three representations (parent → term_id; variation → slug string; lookup table → term_id again). Local attributes excluded from filtering (// Custom product attribute, not suitable for attribute-based filtering.). No validation of a variation's value against the parent's list: "option":"Mint" → 201, stored attribute_pa_flavour='mint', no term created.

No retrieved artifact declares a selection axis or a generated grid: \b(axis|axes|variationTheme)\b → 0 over 5,387 files (the 59 naive hits are all taxes). Nearest construct is a property of the ordinary definition: attributeConstraint ∈ {None, Unique, CombinationUnique, SameForAll} — “CombinationUnique: … should have different combinations in each variant. Use this constraint for variant dimensions such as color and size.” Hedges: scoped four different ways across the vendor's pages; not checked when an attribute is removed; the vendor's own reference dataset sets color/size to None (0 CombinationUnique across 21 definitions); whether any object stores a family's axes is unresolved (U12).

rows.h: same store, via a per-parent join row
rows.shape: An ordinary EAV attribute becomes an axis by one row scoped to one parent: catalog_product_super_attribute {product_super_attribute_id PK, product_id FK CASCADE, attribute_id (no FK), position; UNIQUE (product_id, attribute_id)} + catalog_product_super_attribute_label {…, store_id, use_default, value varchar(255)}. Eligibility, complete: canUseAttribute() = SCOPE_GLOBAL && getIsVisible() && usesSource() && getIsUserDefined() — consults neither the set, the category nor apply_to. The per-family facts (position, label, per-store label) live on the join row — exactly the “dimension row” shape. Value: an ordinary EAV value, option_id integer in catalog_product_entity_int.value — a shared row referenced by integer. Two enforcement paths disagree: REST POST /V1/configurable-products/:sku/options runs neither canUseAttribute() site (U15); the Admin picker admits a different population. (#11031's “Both” headline is not in the record.)

costs: P1: Amazon “most product facts must be replicated across the family”; Walmart copies the axis value per item; eBay repeats the aspect per member
P2: Shopify options are per product (no shop-level registry); Square is the counter-case — option values shared across items; WooCommerce: three representations of one value
Akeneo: one editor, axis force-added to the set; Magento: a set gate implemented as an auto-fix modal
Square: two mechanisms, neither keyed to what the product is; Shopee: two disjoint namespaces, 0 of 92 records carry both ids
Magento: one value store serves both
Square: separate query classes for options vs custom attributes
Shopee: attribute value typed + unit; variation option a bare label
Shopify shipped linkedMetafield (“early access”); Salesforce migrated away from P1 and says why
